title: Lower cardinality estimate for substring-match table filters
hypothesis: Every non-equality table filter is costed with a flat DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY=0.2 (relation_statistics_helper.cpp:146-151; same constant in relation_manager.cpp:199/258/276/293/374 for filters left in a LogicalFilter). A predicate that requires a literal substring (contains(col,'lit'), col LIKE '%lit%', LIKE '%a%b%') is usually far more selective than a range comparison. Evidence from q09: p_name LIKE '%ghost%' is actually about 5% selective. EXPLAIN estimates 1,256,266 rows for lineitem⋈part⋈orders and 5,057,324 for the top join, but EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 324,507 rows, a 4-15x overestimate. Because of that the optimizer builds hash tables on orders (1.5M rows) and on partsupp⋈supplier⋈nation (800k rows), and each of those two joins costs about 0.22-0.23s CPU, while the real probe side is only 324k rows. With a better estimate the join order and build sides can put the small filtered side on the build side.
plan: In RelationStatisticsHelper::ExtractGetStats (src/optimizer/join_order/relation_statistics_helper.cpp, around lines 119-155), when no equality filter fired, check whether any non-optional table filter is an ExpressionFilter whose expression is a positive substring-containment test: a BoundFunctionExpression named 'contains', or '~~' / 'like_escape' whose constant pattern starts with '%' and contains at least one non-wildcard character, possibly nested under CONJUNCTION_AND. Do not match negations (!~~, NOT). If one is found, use base_cardinality * SUBSTRING_MATCH_SELECTIVITY, defined as DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY*DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY (0.04) in relation_statistics_helper.hpp, instead of 0.2. Apply the same classification in relation_manager.cpp where a LogicalFilter's expressions fall back to DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY: add a small static helper IsSubstringMatchPredicate(const Expression&) to RelationStatisticsHelper and reuse it in both places. Before and after the change, check with EXPLAIN on q09/q16 that the estimates move and that the join order changes. Run the full visible bench, since plans may change elsewhere.
expected_gain: q09 (18% of total): possibly 20-40% if the orders/partsupp builds shrink or the join order changes. Smaller effects possible on q16 (s_comment LIKE '%..%..%' under NOT IN) and on other templates with LIKE '%x%' on a dimension table. Roughly 3-8% on the visible geomean if q09 moves.
generality: Any star or snowflake join where a dimension is filtered by a substring/contains predicate (text search on names or comments) now gets a realistic, smaller cardinality, so it is placed on the build side and joined early. Possible regressions: substring predicates that are actually unselective (for example '%a%') will be underestimated, which could put a big relation on the build side. That risk is bounded because the build-side flip and the hash join still work correctly, only slower.
risk: Medium. The change only affects cost estimates, so results stay correct, but plans for other templates may change, possibly for the worse. The selectivity constant is a heuristic derived from DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY, not tuned to the data. If the bench shows a mixed result, try applying it only when the literal has at least 3 characters before giving up.

title: Investigate high-cardinality hash aggregation cost after outer join
hypothesis: In q13, HASH_GROUP_BY on a single integer key (c_custkey) over 1.53M rows into 150k groups costs 0.20s CPU, about 130ns/row and the largest operator in the 2nd slowest template. The group key comes from the build side of a RIGHT join and has tight min/max stats [1,150000]. Each of the 8 threads sees nearly every group (reduction only about 1.3x per thread), so the thread-local tables give little benefit before repartitioning. DecideAdaptation in radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp:424 skips lookups only when the HLL unique share is above 0.95.
plan: First profile only (perf on q13), to see whether the cost is in the local sink, the repartition, or the finalize/combine. Candidate fixes, to be chosen after profiling: (a) when the estimated group count from stats is close to the row count per thread, start in skip-lookup/partition-only mode earlier; (b) a dense-range direct aggregation path for a single integer key with a small stats range and simple aggregates. Do not change the perfect_ht_threshold default, which is a setting.
expected_gain: q13 maybe 20-30%. Any template with a GROUP BY on a high-cardinality key (q18 subquery GROUP BY l_orderkey) may also benefit.
generality: GROUP BY on a high-cardinality key with low per-thread reduction, a common pattern in analytical queries (per-customer or per-order aggregates).
risk: Medium-high. The aggregate hash table is heavily tuned, so a constant tweak can regress low-cardinality aggregates. It needs a profile before any coding.

title: Substring-match scan selectivity (minimal, finish E0001)
hypothesis: q09 (123.8ms, slowest template) builds hash joins on orders (1.5M) and partsupp (800k) while the real probe side is about 324k rows. The cause is that the part scan filter contains(p_name,'ghost'), pushed down from LIKE '%ghost%', is estimated at DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY 0.2 (about 40k rows), but only about 5% of rows pass. EXPLAIN shows estimates of about 1.26M rows for lineitem⋈part⋈orders and 5.06M for the top join. E0001 did not fail as an idea: the implementer ran out of time while building, and it was never benchmarked. If the part estimate drops to about 8k, the join-order optimizer should make the filtered part/lineitem side the build side.
plan: Keep the diff small and out of the header, so the rebuild stays short. In src/optimizer/join_order/relation_statistics_helper.cpp, add a file-local static helper IsSubstringMatchFilter(const TableFilter&). It returns true for an ExpressionFilter whose expression is contains(col, non-empty VARCHAR constant), or ~~/like_escape with a constant pattern that starts with '%' and contains a literal character. It recurses into ConjunctionAndFilter children. It never matches OR, NOT or !~~. In ExtractGetStats (around lines 146-151), when no equality filter applied and some non-optional table filter matches, use selectivity 0.04 (a file-local constexpr) instead of DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY. Leave relation_manager.cpp unchanged in this experiment. Then: build in the background, EXPLAIN q09.m0 and confirm the part estimate falls to about 8k and the join order changes, then run the full bench.
expected_gain: q09: 20-40% if the build sides flip. Other templates with LIKE '%x%' filters on a dimension table (q13-like, q16, q14 variants) may change their plans. Geomean: 1-3%.
generality: Any query with a substring LIKE or contains filter on a table that is joined. Substring filters are usually much more selective than 0.2. A query whose substring filter matches most rows could get a worse join order, since the estimate would be about 5x too low.
risk: Low-medium. Only estimates change, so results stay correct. Plan changes on hidden templates could regress some. Mitigation if results are mixed: apply the lower selectivity only when the literal is at least 3 characters.

title: Cardinality-aware perfect hash aggregation above the bit threshold
hypothesis: q13 (the second-slowest template, about 97ms) spends 0.20s CPU in HASH_GROUP_BY on a single integer key (c_custkey, stats [1,150000], 18 bits) over 1.53M rows into 150k groups. The radix hash table gets little benefit from thread-local pre-aggregation here, because each thread sees most of the groups. CanUsePerfectHashAggregate (src/execution/physical_plan/plan_aggregate.cpp:127) refuses perfect hashing because 18 bits is more than perfect_ht_threshold (12). I measured this directly with `SET perfect_ht_threshold=20`: the plan becomes PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY at 0.04s CPU, and the hot wall time of the q13 inner query falls from about 107ms to about 73ms (-30%). Counter-evidence that makes a guard necessary: the q18-style `GROUP BY l_orderkey HAVING sum(l_quantity)>300` over lineitem (23 bits, 1.5M groups, 6M rows) goes from 76ms to 800-1040ms with threshold 24. Each thread allocates and initialises a 2^bits table, and the global Combine and the scan are O(2^bits) and serial. So perfect hashing pays off only when the dense table is small compared with the input.
plan: In plan_aggregate.cpp only, with no header changes and the setting's default unchanged: keep the existing check (perfect_hash_bits <= perfect_ht_threshold, which accepts as today). When that check fails, accept anyway if all of the following hold: (1) perfect_hash_bits <= a file-local constexpr cap of 20 bits (1M slots); (2) the aggregate child's estimated_cardinality is known and (1 << perfect_hash_bits) * number_of_threads <= 2 * estimated_cardinality (the per-thread tables are no larger than about twice the input, so allocation, initialisation and combine stay proportional to the input); (3) every other existing condition holds (no grouping sets, no DISTINCT, combine callback present). CanUsePerfectHashAggregate needs the estimate passed in from CreatePlan(LogicalAggregate&) via op.children[0]->estimated_cardinality, and the thread count from TaskScheduler::GetScheduler(context).NumberOfThreads(). If the user set perfect_ht_threshold above the default, the existing check already covers it. Steps: build in the background; EXPLAIN q13.m0 and confirm PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY; EXPLAIN q18.m0 and confirm its large GROUP BY stays HASH_GROUP_BY; then run the full bench. If q13 improves but the estimate is too far off in other cases, tighten the factor of 2 to 1.
expected_gain: q13 about 25-30% (about 97ms → about 70ms), roughly a 2% geomean gain from one template. Any template with GROUP BY on a 13-20 bit dense integer key over many more rows (q18-style per-key aggregates with smaller key ranges, per-customer or per-supplier aggregates) also benefits.
generality: GROUP BY on one or more integer keys with min/max stats whose dense range (2^13 to 2^20) is small compared with the input row count: per-entity aggregates over fact tables after joins to dimension keys. Queries whose estimates are badly wrong (estimate high, actual input small) could get slower from allocating 1M-slot tables per thread. The cap of 20 bits bounds that cost to a few MB per thread.
risk: Low-medium. The diff is one file and planner-only, and it reuses an existing, tested operator, so the risk to correctness is low. The performance risk comes from overestimated cardinality; measured, a 23-bit case was 10x slower, which is why the hard cap and the guard on the ratio to input size exist. The reviewer may ask whether this circumvents the setting. The argument is that the setting is still honoured as the unconditional threshold, and the new rule only adds a cost-based acceptance.

title: Lazy-initialised perfect hash aggregate table with a bounded bit extension
hypothesis: E0003 showed that perfect hashing q13's inner aggregate (18 bits, 1.53M rows, 150k groups) saves about 25% wall time (115->90ms, agg CPU 0.20s->0.04s). It also showed that estimate-based acceptance fails: q13 is underestimated 5x and q17 overestimated 1000x. q17 regressed because PerfectAggregateHashTable's constructor (perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp:28-48) eagerly calls InitializeStates on all 2^bits slots in every thread, and Combine (:163) and Destroy (:289) walk all 2^bits slots. If states are initialised only on first touch, a perfect table on a near-empty input costs one uninitialised malloc and a memset of 2^bits bool flags, so a cardinality-independent bit cap becomes safe for small inputs.
plan: 1) perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp constructor: keep the uninitialised data allocation and the group_is_set memset, and remove the InitializeStates loop. 2) AddChunk (:132-142): when group_is_set[group] is false, set it to true and append the slot address to a new-groups address vector, then call RowOperations::InitializeStates once for those new slots before UpdateStates. Flag first, so a duplicate in the same chunk is not initialised twice. 3) Combine: when the target slot is not set, InitializeStates the target first (batch new targets the same way), then CombineStates. Add a touched-groups counter as a member in perfect_aggregate_hashtable.hpp, incremented on first touch. If other.touched == 0, return early (still move the allocator). Otherwise scan group_is_set 8 bytes at a time (memcpy into uint64_t and skip zero words). 4) Destroy: call destructors only on slots with group_is_set (only those are initialised). 5) Scan: the same word-skip over group_is_set. 6) plan_aggregate.cpp CanUsePerfectHashAggregate (:230): keep the PerfectHtThresholdSetting check, but also accept when total bits <= 18 and 2^bits * an estimated row width stays below about 8MB per thread. Use a file-local constexpr. Do NOT change the setting's default. Build in the background, check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that q13's inner aggregate becomes PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY, then run the full bench and look closely at q17, q14 and q18.
expected_gain: q13 about -20% (measured with a forced SET in E0003). Small gains on other GROUP BYs over dense integer keys with 13-18 bits (E0003 quick bench hinted at q02, q03, q07). Geomean maybe 2-3%.
generality: Any GROUP BY on integer keys with a stats range of 4k-262k values (customer, part, supplier and date keys), which is common in analytics. Lazy init also helps existing <=12-bit perfect aggregates on tiny inputs. Could get slower: aggregates with a wide stats range but very sparse actual groups and large inputs (random access over a table up to 8MB instead of a compact HT), and plans with many tiny overestimated aggregates (each pays a 262KB memset per thread).
risk: Medium. Correctness: every state must be initialised before Update, Combine or Finalize, and Destroy must skip uninitialised slots (aggregates with destructors, e.g. list or string min/max). The header change rebuilds a moderate number of files. The 18-bit cap must hold, because 23 bits was measured 10x slower.

title: Per-key bloom filter pushdown for multi-key hash joins
hypothesis: In q09 (the slowest template, 114ms) the 2-key join partsupp ⋈ (filtered part/lineitem build side, ~324k rows) probes all 800k partsupp rows. Its probe costs ~0.14-0.16s CPU, and the scan only gets min/max dynamic filters, because JoinFilterPushdownInfo::CanUseBloomFilter (physical_hash_join.cpp:775) requires ht->conditions.size()==1. The only reason is that the HT bloom filter is filled with the combined hash of all keys (JoinHashTable::Finalize join_hashtable.cpp:790 loads the stored row hash, and InsertHashes :721 inserts it into bloom_filter). BFTableFilter::Filter (bloom_filter.cpp:90-92) probes with VectorOperations::Hash of the single filter column. A BF on one key column needs that column hashed on its own. ps_partkey alone is very selective here, since p_name LIKE '%ghost%' keeps ~5% of parts. A partkey BF would drop ~95% of partsupp rows in the scan before the probe and the hash computation. The SelectivityOptionalFilter wrapper (BF_THRESHOLD/BF_CHECK_N) already switches off a BF on an unselective key such as ps_suppkey, so pushing a filter on every equality key is safe.
plan: 1) join_hashtable.hpp/.cpp: keep the existing single-key bloom_filter path as it is. Add per-key bloom filters for multi-key equality joins, e.g. `vector<unique_ptr<BloomFilter>> key_bloom_filters` indexed by condition index, plus setter/getter. In AllocatePointerTable (:741), Initialize each requested one with Count(). In Finalize (:775), for each requested key: Gather that key column from row_locations into a Vector (data_collection->Gather with an incremental sel, as at :968/:1487). First verify which layout column holds condition i; equality keys may be reordered (see equality_predicate_columns). Then VectorOperations::Hash it into a hash vector and call key_bf.InsertHashes(hash_vec, count). Only do this work when a key BF was requested. 2) physical_hash_join.cpp: in CanUseBloomFilter, allow conditions.size()>1 when cmp == COMPARE_EQUAL (keep the build_side_has_filter and probe-larger checks). In FinalizeFilters (:899), for multi-key joins, record the condition index join_condition[filter_idx] in the deferred entry and request the key BF for that condition. In PushBloomFilter (:787), for multi-key joins, use that condition's BF, NullValuesAreEqual(cond_idx), conditions[cond_idx].right->ToString() and left->return_type instead of index 0. The deferred vector's pair type may need a third field (a struct or tuple), so update the declarations at physical_hash_join.cpp:212 and join_filter_pushdown.hpp:86. 3) Before the full bench, check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE of q09 that the partsupp scan shows an 'IN BF' dynamic filter on ps_partkey, and that its row count falls from 800k to under 100k. Build in the background, since join_hashtable.hpp is included by the join operators.
expected_gain: q09: 10-20% (partsupp probe ~0.15s CPU plus scan and hash work on 800k rows). Small gains are possible on other multi-key equality joins where the build side is filtered. Geomean maybe -1.5% to -3%.
generality: Any equi-join on a composite key (partsupp/lineitem-style composite keys, multi-column fact-to-dimension joins, decorrelated subqueries correlated on 2+ columns) where the build side is filtered. Possible slowdowns: multi-key joins with large unselective build sides pay an extra gather, hash and BF insert per key on the build. The check that the probe is larger than the build, and SelectivityOptionalFilter on the probe side, limit this.
risk: Medium. Correctness depends on mapping each condition index to its layout column and on matching hash semantics. The BF must hash exactly like VectorOperations::Hash on the probe column type; skip keys whose probe column has a cast (has_cast is already checked). NULL handling must use the per-condition NullValuesAreEqual. A header change means a longer rebuild.

title: Collapse adjacent duplicate group keys before hash-table probe in aggregation
hypothesis: q18 (87ms, 3rd slowest) is dominated by the subquery `SELECT l_orderkey FROM lineitem GROUP BY l_orderkey HAVING sum(l_quantity)>312`. Measured with dbe-tool sql: that aggregate takes ~65-72ms hot. A plain sum(l_quantity) scan of lineitem takes 3ms, so nearly all of the time is in GroupedAggregateHashTable (6M rows, 1.5M groups). lineitem is stored clustered by l_orderkey (about 4 consecutive rows per key), so roughly 75% of input rows have the same group key as the row before them. Today each of those rows still pays the full FindOrCreateGroupsInternal path (aggregate_hashtable.cpp:641-814): offset/salt computation, the inner probe loop with a random cache-missing access into `entries`, and a RowMatcher compare against the materialized group row. If equal adjacent keys are detected with a cheap sequential compare of the input vector, only the run heads need to be probed, and the other rows copy the head's address. Clustered or sorted keys are common: order ids, time-series ingestion order, and join outputs that keep probe-side order (for example GROUP BY l_orderkey after a join probed by lineitem in q03-style queries).
plan: In src/execution/aggregate_hashtable.cpp, GroupedAggregateHashTable::FindOrCreateGroupsInternal, after the hashes and addresses vectors are flattened and before the probe loop (i.e. not in the skip_lookups branch), add a file-local static helper that builds a selection of run heads. Row r is a duplicate of r-1 when hashes[r]==hashes[r-1] and every group column is equal at r and r-1, checked with the UnifiedVectorFormat already produced by TupleDataCollection::ToUnifiedFormat (state.partitioned_append_state.chunk_state.vector_data): null-ness must match, and both values are equal or both NULL. Restrict this to group columns of fixed-size physical types (numerics, dates, hugeint) plus string_t compared via Equals; otherwise skip the fast path. If the number of duplicates is 0 (or below about chunk_size/8), use the existing path unchanged. Otherwise run the existing loop with `sel_vector` pointing at a heads SelectionVector and `remaining_entries = head_count` (the inner loop already has a sel_vector->IsSet() template variant, and new_groups_out/empty_vector indices are original row indices, so appends are unaffected). After the loop, fill addresses[r] = addresses[r-1] for each duplicate r in ascending order. Make it adaptive with a member or AggregateHTAppendState counter: after ~16 chunks with less than 1/8 duplicates, disable the check for that hash table, so unclustered inputs pay only a short trial cost. If a new member is needed, put it in AggregateHTAppendState or the GroupedAggregateHashTable header (src/include/duckdb/execution/aggregate_hashtable.hpp) and accept the rebuild; build in the background. UpdateAggregates already handles repeated addresses, as today's path produces them for in-chunk duplicates. Verify q18 with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and check that the results are identical. Also run a GROUP BY with NULL keys and with a multi-column key (l_orderkey, l_linenumber) for correctness.
expected_gain: q18 -15 to -25% (the subquery aggregate is ~70% of its time; probe+compare work drops for ~75% of rows). Small gains are possible on q03, q04 and q18's outer aggregates and on any GROUP BY over join output that keeps lineitem/orders order. Roughly -1.5 to -3% visible geomean.
generality: Any hash aggregate (and DISTINCT, which shares FindOrCreateGroups) whose input has runs of equal keys: sorted or clustered tables, data loaded in time order, joins that keep probe order, and low-cardinality keys in sorted data. Queries on randomly ordered keys pay one sequential compare per row for the first ~16 chunks, after which the check is disabled. That cost is negligible, but tiny aggregates with a high chunk count over random data could see under 1% overhead.
risk: Medium-low. The logic is local to one function and correctness is easy to test (results must match exactly). The main risks are NULL handling in the adjacency compare and interaction with the unpartitioned_data path that uses empty_vector indices. Both are covered by keeping original row indices. Performance risk is small because of the adaptive disable.

title: Contains-filter scan selectivity to flip q09 build sides at SF10
hypothesis: At the new data size (SF10), q09's two most expensive joins have their build side on the larger input. I verified this with `dbe-tool profile q09.m0`, where in HASH_JOIN the right child is the build side. (1) For l_orderkey=o_orderkey, the build is the full orders scan (15M rows) and the probe is lineitem⋈part (3.27M rows); the operator costs 2.97s CPU. (2) For p_partkey=ps_partkey AND l_suppkey=ps_suppkey, the build is partsupp⋈supplier (8M rows) and the probe is the same 3.27M stream; it costs 2.82s CPU. Together these are about 5.8s of q09's roughly 10s CPU. Two things cause this. The part scan filter contains(p_name,'ghost') gets the flat DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY of 0.2, so part is estimated at 400k rows while the actual count is 109k. That makes lineitem⋈part about 12M estimated versus 3.27M actual, which is comparable to orders (15M) and larger than partsupp (8M), so the optimizer builds on orders and partsupp. With selectivity 0.04 the estimate becomes about 2.4M. That is far below both 15M and 8M, so the build-probe optimizer should put the 3.27M side on the build side of both joins. orders (15M) and partsupp (8M) would then become probes and get bloom/min-max filters. E0002 tested exactly this code at SF1 and saw no plan change, because at SF1 orders was already the probe side. The data size has changed the situation since then.
plan: Re-implement E0002's minimal change, restricted to contains(). In src/optimizer/join_order/relation_statistics_helper.cpp, add a file-local static `IsContainsFilter(const TableFilter&)`. It returns true for an ExpressionFilter whose expression is a BoundFunctionExpression named "contains" with a non-empty VARCHAR constant argument. It also recurses into ConjunctionAndFilter children. Look up the actual filter classes in src/planner/filter/ (expression_filter, conjunction_filter) and handle OPTIONAL_FILTER the same way as the surrounding code. Do NOT match prefix(), suffix(), LIKE with a single leading %, NOT, or OR. Suffix patterns like '%BRASS' are genuinely about 0.2 selective. In ExtractGetStats (around line 146-151), when there is no equality filter and a non-optional filter is a contains filter, use 0.2*0.2 instead of DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY. Keep the change out of headers, i.e. file-local constexpr. STEP 1, before the bench: build in the background, then run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on q09.m0 with `dbe-tool sql`. Confirm that the l_orderkey join now has the lineitem/part side as the build (right child) and orders as the probe, and the same for partsupp. If the plan does not flip, look at src/optimizer/build_probe_side_optimizer.cpp to see why (width or cost terms), report that, and stop. STEP 2: run the full bench.
expected_gain: q09 (24% of total time, 1.2s): if both joins flip, the hash table builds go from 15M+8M rows down to 2×3.27M, and orders and partsupp get bloom-filtered probes. Expected 30-50% faster on q09. Other templates are unchanged unless they have a contains filter.
generality: Any query with a '%word%' LIKE or contains() filter on a dimension table that is joined to a fact table. Substring matches are almost always much more selective than 20%. It could get slower when a contains literal is very unselective, such as a single common character, which could flip a join the wrong way. A fallback option is to apply it only for literals of 3 or more characters.
risk: Low-medium. The diff only changes estimates in one file. The main risk is plan changes in hidden templates that use contains filters. E0002 already showed that this code builds and moves the estimates as intended.

title: Per-key bloom filter for multi-key joins, revived for the post-E0008 q09 plan
hypothesis: Since E0008 flipped the q09 plan at SF10, lineitem (59,986,045 rows, scan 3.60s CPU) is the PROBE side of a 2-key join (l_partkey = p_partkey AND l_suppkey = ps_suppkey). The BUILD side is part⋈partsupp: 435,892 rows, about 109k distinct partkeys out of 2M. That join costs 2.44s CPU and emits only 3,269,453 rows (5.4%). The lineitem scan gets only min/max dynamic filters, because JoinFilterPushdownInfo::CanUseBloomFilter (physical_hash_join.cpp:761-785) requires ht->conditions.size()==1. A bloom filter on the l_partkey key alone would cut the scan output from 60M to about 3.3M rows before the hash probe. E0005 built exactly this but was rejected because its premise was wrong for the OLD plan, where partsupp was the build side and lineitem was already filtered. In the current plan the premise holds, as verified by `dbe-tool profile q09.m0` this round. Its regressions (q19 +48%, q22 +21%) shrank to +9.9%/+4% on re-run, and q19 has only single-key joins, so they were most likely noise. Re-check them anyway.
plan: Re-implement E0005's per-key bloom filter (see ledger E0005 for its design). JoinHashTable keeps one BloomFilter per equality condition index, initialised in AllocatePointerTable. Finalize fills it by gathering layout column cond_idx, running VectorOperations::Hash on it and calling InsertHashes. In CanUseBloomFilter, allow conditions.size()>1 when this condition is COMPARE_EQUAL, but keep build_side_has_filter and probe_larger_then_build. The deferred bloom-filter entries in FinalizeFilters (physical_hash_join.cpp:~814-900) carry the condition index, and PushBloomFilter uses that condition's BF, null semantics (NullValuesAreEqual(cond_idx)), key name and type. Keep wrapping it in SelectivityOptionalFilter so that a key that filters nothing (l_suppkey here) switches itself off at runtime. To bound build cost, build per-key BFs only for single-column equality conditions, at most 2 per join. Keep changes in .cpp files where possible; if a header must change (join_hashtable.hpp), build in the background. STEP 1: EXPLAIN ANALYZE q09.m0 and confirm the lineitem scan shows `l_partkey IN BF(...)` and emits far fewer than 60M rows. STEP 2: run the full bench, then re-run q18, q19 and q22 to rule out the E0005-era regressions.
expected_gain: q09 (709ms, the slowest template): the 2.44s-CPU join probe drops to about 0.2s and the 3.6s lineitem scan sheds most of its downstream work. Expect q09 -25 to -40% and geomean -2 to -3%. Other templates: neutral unless they have a multi-key equality join with a filtered build side.
generality: Any star or snowflake query that joins a big fact table to a filtered dimension on a composite key (partsupp-style bridge tables, (date, store) or (order, line) keys). Possible slowdowns: multi-key joins whose build side is large and unselective, which pay for building the BF and for about BF_CHECK_N chunks of probe hashing before SelectivityOptionalFilter turns it off.
risk: Medium. NULL semantics per condition, condition-index bookkeeping after ReorderConditions (E0005's notes say indices match op.conditions == ht->conditions), and extra build-side hashing. E0005's code was reviewed as correct, which lowers the implementation risk.

title: Derive per-table OR filters when the OR sits under a root AND (JoinDependentFilterRule after distributivity)
hypothesis: In q19 (347ms, the 4th slowest template), the part scan has NO filters: 2M rows go into the build side. The lineitem scan has no l_quantity filter: 15M rows probe the join (0.62s CPU), then a 0.39s FILTER evaluates the big OR and leaves 1,170 rows. JoinDependentFilterRule (src/optimizer/rule/join_dependent_filter.cpp) exists to derive per-table filters from an OR of ANDs, but Apply() returns early unless the OR is the ROOT expression (is_root). DistributivityRule is registered first (optimizer.cpp:52, vs :69) and factors the common terms (p_partkey=l_partkey, l_shipmode, l_shipinstruct) out of q19's OR, so the root becomes AND(common..., OR(rest)). The rule never fires. The same happens whenever a WHERE has an OR of cross-table ANDs plus other conjuncts, for example the q07 shape (n1='FRANCE' AND n2='GERMANY') OR (n1='GERMANY' AND n2='FRANCE') alongside join predicates. EVIDENCE: I appended the derived filters by hand: AND ((p_brand=.. AND p_container IN .. AND p_size BETWEEN ..) OR ...x3) AND ((l_quantity>=9 AND l_quantity<=19) OR ...x3). q19 went from 358ms to 173/181ms hot with the same result (41150783.5184). The part build shrinks to a few thousand rows, which also lets a join BF reach the lineitem scan.
plan:
In src/optimizer/rule/join_dependent_filter.cpp only:
(1) Move the derivation (ExtractConjunctedExpressions per child, then intersect the table indices across all children, building OR-of-per-table-ANDs) out of Apply into a file-local static `unique_ptr<Expression> DeriveFilter(BoundConjunctionExpression &or_expr)`. It returns nullptr when it is not eligible or derives nothing. Keep the existing eligibility check: at least one child is an AND that references several tables.
(2) In Apply, keep the op-type and is_root checks. If the root is CONJUNCTION_OR, behave exactly as today. If the root is CONJUNCTION_AND, loop over its direct children. For each child that is CONJUNCTION_OR, call DeriveFilter. Flatten the result into individual derived conjuncts, and keep each one only if no existing child of the root AND is Equals() to it. This dedupe is REQUIRED: the rewriter re-applies rules until fixpoint, and without it the rule loops forever. If anything was added, return a copy of the root AND with the new children appended and set changes_made. Otherwise return nullptr.
(3) The root matcher (a ConjunctionExpressionMatcher with SOME child conjunction) already matches an AND with an OR child, so no matcher change should be needed. Verify this.
CHECK BEFORE THE BENCH: EXPLAIN q19.m0 must show the p_brand/p_container/p_size OR filter on the part scan and an l_quantity filter on the lineitem scan. Run q19 and q07 and compare results with the current build. Confirm the planner finishes (no rewriter loop) on q19, q07 and a query with nested ORs. No header changes and no setting changes.
expected_gain: q19 about -45 to -50% (measured 358 -> ~177ms with manually derived filters), which is about -4% on the geomean by itself. q07 may gain if its nation OR is in the same AND-rooted shape. Other templates are unaffected.
generality: Any query whose WHERE/join filter has an OR of ANDs across tables alongside other conjuncts, or where distributivity factored out common terms. This is common in BI-generated filters and multi-segment predicates. The derived filters are implied by the original predicate, so results cannot change. Possible slowdown: the derived filters are evaluated in addition to the original OR. When they are unselective, that adds a small scan-filter cost, about what the existing root-OR path already accepts.
risk: Low-medium. The diff is contained to one file. The main risk is non-termination in the rewriter fixpoint loop if the dedupe is wrong, so test planning on several OR queries. Smaller risks: duplicated expressions, and cardinality estimates that change join order elsewhere. Wrong results are impossible as long as the derived terms are only ANDed onto the original.

title: Deliminator: drop the delim join for SEMI/ANTI subqueries without blocking operators even when the LHS has a selection
hypothesis: q04 (319ms, 4th slowest) runs EXISTS as a RIGHT_DELIM_JOIN (0.30s) + INNER join lineitem x DELIM_SCAN (0.17s) + RIGHT_SEMI join (0.17s) + a dedup HASH_GROUP_BY on the delim side. Deliminator::Optimize (src/optimizer/deliminator.cpp:66) deliberately keeps the deepest join with the DelimGet when HasSelection(delim_join) is true (orders has a date filter). The idea is that the delim set reduces expensive RHS work. For a plain EXISTS/NOT EXISTS whose RHS is only scans, filters and projections, that reduction buys nothing a single hash semi/anti join does not already do. MANUAL REWRITE TEST: q04 written as `orders SEMI JOIN (SELECT l_orderkey FROM lineitem WHERE l_commitdate<l_receiptdate)` gives the same result in 283/220/210ms hot, against 303/~300ms for the EXISTS form. A q22-style NOT EXISTS (customer with a filter, anti join to orders) went from 89ms to 61/63ms with the same count of 27085.
plan: In Deliminator::Optimize (deliminator.cpp:58-71), compute `keep_deepest = !candidate.joins.empty() && HasSelection(delim_join)` as now, then add an exception. Set keep_deepest = false when (a) delim_join.join_type is JoinType::SEMI or JoinType::ANTI, and (b) the RHS subtree delim_join.children[1] contains no LOGICAL_AGGREGATE_AND_GROUP_BY, LOGICAL_WINDOW, LOGICAL_LIMIT, LOGICAL_ORDER_BY, LOGICAL_TOP_N, LOGICAL_DISTINCT or nested LOGICAL_DELIM_JOIN. Write (b) as a file-local static recursive helper, not a header change. In those cases the delim provides no pruning before a blocking operator. Keep everything else unchanged, so scalar or aggregate subqueries (q02, q17, q20) still keep the deepest join. Validate: EXPLAIN q04 should show a single HASH_JOIN SEMI/RIGHT_SEMI between orders and lineitem with no RIGHT_DELIM_JOIN. Check that the condition is plain equality, or that IS NOT DISTINCT FROM does not block the BF or perfect HT, and whether a join BF/min-max filter reaches the lineitem scan. Compare results for q04, q21 and q22 with the old build. Also try EXISTS with an extra correlated inequality, and NOT EXISTS with NULL keys (check that the IS NOT NULL filter handling at :217-225 stays correct for ANTI). Then bench.
expected_gain: q04 about -25% (300 -> about 215ms), and q22 if its NOT EXISTS has this shape (ANTI test -30%). About -2 to -3% visible geomean. Hidden EXISTS/NOT EXISTS/IN-without-aggregate templates (q21-like, q16 NOT IN maybe) also stand to gain.
generality: Any correlated EXISTS / NOT EXISTS / IN subquery with simple equality correlation and a filtered outer table. This is a very common analytical pattern. Could get slower: cases where the RHS is a multi-join chain, because the preserved inner join with the delim set acted as an early filter for joins higher in the RHS. Join BFs and dynamic filters should mostly cover that, which is why condition (b) excludes blocking operators but allows joins. If a regression shows up, tighten (b) to also forbid joins in the RHS.
risk: Low-medium. It is a one-file optimizer heuristic change that reuses the existing removal path, which is already exercised whenever the LHS has no selection, so correctness risk is small (the main checks are ANTI and NULL semantics). Performance risk is limited to the multi-join-RHS case described above.

title: Join filters (min-max + bloom) for RIGHT_SEMI/RIGHT_ANTI probes and equality for deliminated EXISTS conditions
hypothesis: After E0011, q04 runs as one HASH_JOIN RIGHT_SEMI: probe = lineitem (37.9M rows after l_commitdate<l_receiptdate, from a 60M scan), build = filtered orders (574k rows). The join takes 0.89s CPU and the lineitem scan gets NO dynamic or bloom filter. There are two blockers, both verified in code. (1) JoinFilterPushdownOptimizer::GenerateJoinFilters (src/optimizer/join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp:207-219) returns early for RIGHT_SEMI and RIGHT_ANTI. That is overly conservative: in both types the output comes from the build side, so a probe row whose key is not in the build can never affect the result. Only left ANTI, MARK, SINGLE, LEFT and OUTER really need every probe row. (2) The deliminated delim join keeps its condition as `o_orderkey IS NOT DISTINCT FROM o_orderkey`, and GenerateJoinFilters skips COMPARE_NOT_DISTINCT_FROM (line 237). In Deliminator::RemoveJoinWithDelimGet (deliminator.cpp:245-253), each removed plain =/<> correlation condition already adds an IS NOT NULL filter on the subquery-side column. With the RHS key known non-NULL, NOT DISTINCT FROM is equivalent to = for SEMI, ANTI and INNER (a NULL LHS key matches nothing either way). Manual test: rewriting q04 as an explicit SEMI JOIN with = gives the same RIGHT_SEMI plan, still unfiltered because of blocker (1), and 182-210ms vs 214ms. So blocker (2) alone gains little, and the main gain needs (1). The build covers about 3 months of 7 years of orders, so a bloom filter on l_orderkey should cut the probe rows about 15-25x.
plan: A. src/optimizer/join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp GenerateJoinFilters: remove RIGHT_SEMI and RIGHT_ANTI from the early-return list. Keep MARK, SINGLE, LEFT, OUTER and ANTI, and update the comment to say why the right-variants are safe. Leave compute_aggregates_anyway INNER-only, so the perfect-HT behaviour does not change. Check physical_hash_join.cpp (Sink line 339, Finalize 1006-1025) and the bloom filter code (CanUseBloomFilter/PushBloomFilter) for join-type assumptions. B. src/optimizer/deliminator.cpp Deliminator::Optimize: when the candidate is fully removed (the type is changed to LOGICAL_COMPARISON_JOIN at line 109) and every removed correlation condition was a plain COMPARE_EQUAL (so an IS NOT NULL filter was added for each delim column), rewrite the delim_join conditions from COMPARE_NOT_DISTINCT_FROM to COMPARE_EQUAL. Do this only for join_type SEMI, ANTI or INNER, and track it with a local flag. Do not do it if any removed condition was NOT DISTINCT FROM or DISTINCT FROM. Use file-local statics only, with no header changes. Validate with EXPLAIN ANALYZE of q04.m0: the lineitem scan should show a dynamic/bloom filter on l_orderkey and far fewer than 37.9M rows into the join. Also check q22 and q18, where the IN subquery may be RIGHT_SEMI. Correctness: NOT EXISTS and EXISTS with NULL keys on both sides, a RIGHT_ANTI case where the build has keys absent from the probe, and an IN subquery, all checked against unoptimized results (SET disabled_optimizers='join_filter_pushdown').
expected_gain: q04 207ms -> roughly 120-150ms (the join is 0.89s CPU, and most of the lineitem scan/filter feeding it is avoidable). q22 and q18 possibly, if their semi/anti joins are right-flipped. Geomean about 2-4%. Hidden EXISTS, NOT EXISTS and IN templates (TPC-H q20/q21-like) likely benefit.
generality: Any EXISTS, IN or NOT EXISTS subquery, or explicit semi/anti join, where the optimizer puts the small outer side on the build (RIGHT_SEMI/RIGHT_ANTI) and the big table on the probe. That is a very common analytical pattern. Possible slowdowns: unselective filters add bloom/min-max probing cost on scans, but the existing selectivity-based runtime disable mitigates that, the same as for INNER joins.
risk: Medium-low. Correctness risk is in part B's NULL semantics (limited to fully-deliminated joins whose correlation conditions were all plain equality with IS NOT NULL added) and in any hidden join-type assumption in the physical filter code. The diff is small and in two .cpp files.

title: Perfect hash join for RIGHT joins on dense integer keys (range up to 4M)
hypothesis: q13 is the slowest template (773ms, 18.7% of total). Its customer LEFT JOIN orders runs as a physical RIGHT hash join: orders is the probe (14.8M rows), customer the build (1.5M rows, c_custkey dense in [1,1.5M]). The join costs 2.06s CPU. Each probe goes through the pointer table (about 16MB) and then compares keys in the row data, so it pays two random cache misses. PerfectHashJoinExecutor::CanDoPerfectHashJoin (perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp:73) only accepts INNER joins, and MAX_BUILD_SIZE=1048576 at :108 is a file-local constant, not a setting. So q13 is excluded twice: by join type (RIGHT) and by range (1.5M). A perfect probe indexes directly into gathered key vectors (6MB of uinteger keys for q13), with no hashing and no pointer chasing. RIGHT join probe output is the same as INNER output (the matched pairs). The only extra work is recording which build slots matched, so that the existing full-outer scan can emit unmatched build rows. Separately verified this round: in q09, compressed materialization does block the o_orderkey BF from reaching the orders scan, but with CM disabled the BF cut orders from 15M to 2.96M rows and q09 wall time was unchanged (560 vs 560ms). That direction is dead, which is why q13 is the target.
plan:
In src/execution/operator/join/perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp:
(1) CanDoPerfectHashJoin: also accept JoinType::RIGHT, with 1 COMPARE_EQUAL integer condition as today.
(2) Range limit: keep MAX_BUILD_SIZE=1M for the existing INNER rule. Add MAX_DENSE_BUILD_SIZE = 1<<22. A range in (1M, 4M] is allowed only if ht.Count()*2 >= range+1 (at least 50% dense). A RIGHT join of any range also requires that density, so sparse builds and builds where a BF would help stay on the normal HT.
(3) RIGHT match tracking: FullScanHashTable already gathers key_locations (the row pointers). Keep a per-slot row-pointer array and a uint8 matched-flag array, sized by build_size. In ProbePerfectHashTable (:269), when op.join_type==RIGHT, set matched[idx]=1 for each matching probe row (benign race; same as the existing HT found_match writes).
(4) Before the full-outer scan, copy matched flags into the rows' found_match field: one pass over the slots, writing through the stored pointers. Then the existing PhysicalHashJoin full-outer scan source path (physical_hash_join.cpp, ScanFullOuter / the HT's found-match offset) runs unchanged. Hook this where the probe phase finishes and the outer scan starts. Verify the HT actually checks those flags for perfect-HT joins.
(5) Build rows with NULL keys (kept in the HT for RIGHT joins) must not go into a slot. They must stay unmatched so the outer scan emits them. Check how FullScanHashTable handles them today (it may bail out or fail).
The probe output path stays the INNER one. Do not touch LEFT/OUTER/SEMI/ANTI/MARK.
Before the full bench: run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on q13.m0 and confirm the join time drops. Correctness: compare against SET disabled_optimizers='join_filter_pushdown' and the plain HT on a RIGHT join with NULL build keys, duplicate build keys (must fall back), an empty build, unmatched build rows, a negative-key range, multi-column payloads, and customer LEFT JOIN orders with count(o_orderkey) (q13 shape).
expected_gain: q13: join CPU from 2.06s to about 0.8-1.0s, so about 10-20% wall on q13 (about 1.5% geomean). Other templates mostly unchanged, unless an INNER join has a 1-4M dense build (customer at SF10 when unfiltered).
generality: Helps any outer join where the preserved side is a dense-keyed dimension table: the planner puts it on the build side as RIGHT, as in the per-customer, per-part and per-supplier counts with LEFT JOIN that are common in reporting. It also helps INNER joins with dense builds of 1-4M keys. Could get slower: RIGHT joins where the perfect HT replaces a selective bloom filter (gated by the 50% density rule), and very wide build payloads where gathering into vectors costs more than the probe saves.
risk: Medium. RIGHT-join correctness hinges on the found_match handoff to the outer scan and on NULL build keys. The perfect HT disables the BF, which is why the density gate exists. Most of the code is in one .cpp file, and the header change is limited to new members in perfect_hash_join_executor.hpp (not widely included).
